Methodology
Why do the ArcGIS and R outputs look different?
The two pipelines differ at every stage — from how they decide which points are "ground" to how they interpolate a continuous surface. These differences compound, producing noticeably different DSMs, DTMs, and CHMs even from the same raw LiDAR point cloud.
01
Ground classification
ArcGIS Pro

Uses the Progressive Morphological Filter with a "Conservative" setting and a fixed 10 m DEM resolution. The algorithm progressively opens the point cloud using a series of morphological windows, keeping only the lowest points in each window as ground candidates. The conservative mode errs toward classifying points as non-ground to avoid falsely including canopy as terrain.

R (lidR + RCSF)

Uses the Cloth Simulation Filter (CSF) (Zhang et al. 2016). Imagine draping a cloth over an upside-down version of the point cloud and letting it fall under gravity — points close to where the cloth settles are labelled ground. Parameters used: cloth resolution 0.5 m, class threshold 0.5 m, rigidness 2 (medium flexibility), 500 iterations.

Impact on outputs CSF tends to follow terrain more tightly at fine scales, while ArcGIS's conservative PMF may include fewer borderline points as ground. This directly determines what elevation values go into the DTM — and since CHM = DSM − DTM, errors here propagate into canopy height estimates.
02
DTM interpolation
ArcGIS Pro

Uses LAS Dataset to Raster filtered to Class 2 (ground) points. The default interpolation is binning (mean or nearest-neighbour), which averages the elevations of all ground points falling in each output cell. This produces a smoother surface but may not honour individual point positions exactly.

R (lidR)

Uses Delaunay Triangulation (TIN) via rasterize_terrain(algorithm = tin()). Ground points are connected into a mesh of non-overlapping triangles. Triangle size adapts to local point density. Each raster cell is assigned elevation by interpolating within the triangle that contains its centre — this honours every ground point exactly without smoothing.

Impact on outputs TIN interpolation produces sharper terrain features and more faithfully represents micro-topography. ArcGIS binning produces a smoother DTM. In flatter areas like the arboretum, the difference is subtle but visible at the boundary edges and in the slight elevation gradients across the site.
03
DSM construction
ArcGIS Pro

Uses all returns or first returns via LAS Dataset to Raster with the maximum elevation value per cell. This captures the highest surface hit by any pulse in each cell, including multi-return pulses that may have partially penetrated the canopy.

R (lidR)

Uses only first returns — the initial hit of each laser pulse — via rasterize_canopy() applied to the height-normalised point cloud. Because the cloud is first normalised against the TIN-derived DTM, the DSM values represent height above ground directly rather than absolute elevation.

Impact on outputs The R workflow normalises before computing the DSM, meaning the R DSM already represents canopy height rather than absolute elevation. The ArcGIS DSM is in absolute elevation units. This is why the CHM colour scales differ — the R CHM shows pure height (2–23 m) while the ArcGIS CHM works in absolute elevation space before subtraction.
04
CHM derivation
ArcGIS Pro

CHM = DSM − DTM using Raster Calculator. Both inputs are in absolute elevation (metres above sea level), so the subtraction removes terrain and yields height above ground. Output cell size matches both input rasters (1 m).

R (lidR + terra)

Because the point cloud was already height-normalised before DSM creation, the DSM directly equals canopy height above ground. The formal CHM subtraction (DSM − DTM) is still performed but produces nearly identical results to the normalised DSM. Outputs at both 1 m and 0.4 m resolution allow resolution sensitivity analysis.

Impact on outputs The ArcGIS CHM tends to show smoother, lower canopy height estimates because the conservative ground classification retains fewer ground points (raising the DTM slightly) and the binning interpolation smooths fine detail. The R CHM shows sharper, slightly taller canopy peaks because CSF classifies more points as ground (lowering the DTM) and TIN interpolation preserves height variation at fine scales.
